episode_thesis: Jerome Callo argues that a futures program can be orthogonal to trend followers by anticipating the flows of other systematic players (carry, risk parity, vol-control) from term structure, positioning and calendar effects, adding relative-value and slower macro models, and protecting with long-vol and proactive scenario risk limits. He doubts that machine learning adds much on daily financial data because of weak signal-to-noise and non-stationarity.

speakers.role: Founder of DCM Systematic (Geneva), non-trend multi-strategy futures program; ex-BlueTrend quant (2008-2013); PhD in machine learning

worldview_premises.premise: Models simplify a complex reality driven by supply, demand and constraints, so momentum as a single driver is not enough; relative value and behavioural models can add return.
worldview_premises.support: Lesson from BlueTrend and from discretionary traders.

worldview_premises.premise: Trend following has a positive expected return and an optimal blend with it exists, but choosing that blend is the allocator's job; DCM's role is to be non-overlapping.
It is easier to forecast the positioning of large systematic participants (carry, value, momentum, risk parity, trend) than the market, because they cannot unwind large positions quickly.
worldview_premises.support: Reasoning from capacity and unwind time (days); experience from BlueTrend; track record almost nine years.

worldview_premises.premise: Term-structure slope reveals carry-trader positioning because markets do not flip between contango and backwardation overnight.
worldview_premises.support: Found in FX, then worked across asset classes with risk-system adjustments.

worldview_premises.premise: After a two-sigma shock, markets tend to overshoot and normalise within about a week rather than continue.
worldview_premises.support: Own research on commodity and equity shocks.

worldview_premises.premise: Crowded trend and carry positions can be sized by scaling estimated positioning to the whole CTA industry and comparing with CFTC net positions; the best opportunities come when over-traded positions must unwind.
worldview_premises.support: Own positioning estimates plus CFTC data; no numbers given.

worldview_premises.premise: G10 FX returns versus USD are about 80-90% explained by three stable factors; the 10-15% idiosyncratic residual mean-reverts in roughly 10-20 days.
worldview_premises.support: Over 30 years of daily data; PCA gives the same factors.

worldview_premises.premise: Strict market neutrality in relative value forces overtrading or leverage, so slack and some directional exposure are better.
Hedging-role models can earn nothing for years and give false alarms but are kept for their function in shocks; models are judged by portfolio role.
Volatility is the market with the largest exploitable footprint because many traders including retail are short vol; shocks force them out and add convexity.
Seventy-five futures have only about 19 independent degrees of freedom, a compression that has grown since 2008 as markets linked and liquidated together.
worldview_premises.support: Own exercise 'a couple of weeks ago'.

worldview_premises.premise: Machine learning on daily data recovers noisy versions of known signals; finance lacks data volume, has weak signal-to-noise and is not stationary because participants adapt, though some flow patterns such as month-end persist for 20-30 years.
worldview_premises.support: Repeated attempts in research; comparisons with LLMs, recommender systems and protein folding.

worldview_premises.premise: Because participants and structure keep changing, research is continuous and the model set will gain and lose components.

worldview_premises.premise: Adding a trend component to a 25-model non-trend book would probably still raise risk-adjusted returns despite higher correlation to trend followers.
Risk-parity and vol-control funds must cut exposure as prices fall and volatility rises, creating exploitable selling flow for a few days.
Risk premia, factor and bank QIS strategies trade billions on rules and leave predictable footprints.
Month-end effects persist because humans and large pools of capital run monthly schedules and accounting, unlike anomalies that decay once published.
The GSCI and DJ-UBS roll window (business days 5-9) once paid a liquidity premium that has largely decayed as investors spread rolls across the curve.
Proactive risk management stress-tests current positions against past scenarios while reactive risk management adjusts after the fact; VIX is asymmetric (jumps fast, fades slowly).

steps.from: Calendar-based processes of humans and big capital pools

steps.why: Decayed after investors moved to spread-roll implementations

gaps_and_conflicts.issue: Mean-reversion and shock-fade claims (about a week, 10-20 days) have no statistics or sample sizes.
Crowding estimates scaled to the CTA industry are described but no results are given.
The loss constraint 'minus 2%' and Volmageddon +3-4% figure come from the guest, unverified.
Ledger C05-1 overstated; the guest said models gave mixed results in August 2024 and consensus risk is a general concern.
Tension: behavioural signals are said to need no trend, yet shock-fade and long-vol models are partially directional; Jerome concedes some directional exposure is accepted.

forward_looking_inputs: Observable inputs: futures term-structure slope and its change over 5-10 days, estimated CTA/CFTC positioning concentration, two-sigma shocks, VIX term structure and hedging demand, month-end calendar, FX three-factor residuals, inflation prints/nowcast. Horizons: 5-20 days for behavioural and mean-reversion models; one to a few months for macro.
reader_inferences: The case for non-trend alpha rests on a structural argument (known participants must trade predictably) rather than statistical power; it is vulnerable when participants adapt.
Consensus risk across many models makes the portfolio overlay the main unresolved design gap.
Compression to 19 independent bets and cross-asset proxies link diversification limits with signal transfer.
